newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Tunisia says budget deficit in line with inflation.
newsitem.headline: Tunisia says budget deficit in line with inflation.

text.p: The Tunisian government on Tuesday said the 1997 net budget deficit was projected to rise to 640 million dinars from 575 million in 1996 but was still in line with the policy of controlling inflation.

"Thanks to the efforts to mobilise proper resources and from credits, it will be possible to limit the budget deficit within the limit of 640 million dinars and three percent of gross domestic product (GDP)," Prime Minister Hamed Karoui told the parliament in his annual budget speech.
"This is a level compatible...with the continuing of the control of the prices' evolution," he added.
The inflation rate was forecast at 4.2 percent in 1997, unchanged from 1996 estimates.

Karoui also said budget income forecasts took into account a decrease in import taxes because Tunisia will be implementing a free-trade zone accord it signed in 1995 with the European Union by progressively dismantling its customs barriers.

"The forecasts on total incomes were based on the respect of our commitments in the partnership accord with the European Union," Prime Minister Hamed Karoui told the parliament in his annual budget speech.
The draft budget projects total spending of 8.01 billion dinars in 1997, up 10.8 percent from 1996.
Total incomes, 78.4 percent of which would come from fiscal receipts, would be secured through a 4.5-percent increase in tax incomes and 27.6 percent in domestic and foreign borrowings.
"An important part of the customs receipts will be suppressed," as a result of the dismantling of customs barriers, Karoui said without giving a figure.
The government plans to borrow a total 2,546 million dinars in 1997, including 990 million dinars from abroad.
Tunisia's external debt in 1996 stood at 9.745 billion dinars, or 51.5 percent of GDP. It forecasts for 1997 external debt of 10.464 billion dinars, or 49.5 percent of GDP.
Debt servicing was estimated at 1.685 billion dinars, or a ratio of 18.3 percent of current receipts for 1996. In 1997, debt servicing was seen at 1.8 billion.
Karoui said current tax rates would be maintained.
"It wasn't an easy task to conciliate between two essential factors, the credits for the state's expenditures...and the maintaining of the current taxation rates," he said.

The state wage bill is forecast to represent 31 percent of the total budget and increase by 216 million dinars, or 9.5 percent, as a result of the implementation of a salaries increase accord signed in 1996 and of plans to create 9.700 new civil servant jobs.

Despite much talk of reducing the cost of food subsidies, the government has in fact increased the budget allocation to the subsidies fund by 43.2 percent to 348 million dinars from 243 million in 1996.
Development expenditures will amount to 1.675 billion dinars, mainly for infrasturcture projects in the agriculture sector and for roads.
